catalog_quote: [p.5] Tone elements are binary H[igh] and L[ow]. Syllables may be H, L, <HL>, or <LH>, rarely <LHL>. Stems and words may be {H}, {L}, {HL}, {LH}, or {LHL}, with the tone elements spread out over the relevant syllables. There are no lexical tone oppositions among verbs, and only marginal oppositions among adjectives, but nouns may be lexically /HL/, /LH/, or /L/. The general pattern is that at most one syllable in a word is H-toned, so the tonal system has a resemblance to pitch-accent systems that have at most one accented syllable and allow unaccented words. [p.27] In the absence of an elaborated stress/accent system, the distinction between elitics [sic, so printed] and particles is not clearcut. new_statements.rule_in_words: Bunoge is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with no elaborated stress/accent system; word prosody is carried by lexical/grammatical tone melodies (/HL/, /LH/, /L/ for nouns), typically with at most one H per word (pitch accent-like). Phonetically, in H..H.L words the pitch-and-intensity peak falls on the last H syllable, immediately before the H-to-L tone break; Heath floats but does not adopt an accentual reanalysis (initial accent plus rightward H-spreading; /LH/ = final accent; /L/ = unaccented).
new_statements.exceptions: sec. 3.1.2 (p.11): no metrical weakening of medial syllables in CvCvCv; weak (raising/syncope) position is stem-final vowel before certain suffixes. sec. 4.6.1.4 (p.86): before numeral '2' nouns become tonally flat with H plural -gé, producing strings of H syllables that 'go against the pitch accent tendencies of the rest of the language'. Monosyllabic /HL/ and /LH/ nouns have merged (constraint against rising tone on Cv).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the word (noun stems and their tone melodies; clitic diagnosis). The intensity-peak remark is an impressionistic phonetic observation on polysyllabic words, not an instrumental result. Tone overlays (tonosyntax) can replace lexical melodies at phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Bunoge (buno1241) as spoken in Sangou and Boudou villages (western Dogon, near Goundaka), data mainly from one Sangou speaker (2012, 2017) plus Boudou texts (2015). Earlier names: 'budu tagu' (Plungian & Tembine 1994), 'Korandabo' (Hochstetler et al. 2004, actually a greeting). Note the PuRe metadata record mislabels the ISO subject as 'dym Yanda Dom'; the file itself is the Bunoge grammar.

sources.note: Tone language (binary H/L; noun melodies /HL/, /LH/, /L/). No dedicated stress section. p.5: at most one H syllable per word, 'resemblance to pitch accent systems'; p.11 (3.1.2 Metrical structure): no tendency for medial syllable of CvCvCv to weaken; p.27: 'In the absence of an elaborated stress/accent system..'; p.29: peak of pitch and intensity in H.(H.)H.L words is on the syllable just before the tone break, accentual analysis (initial accent + rightward H-spreading) floated but not adopted; p.86: strings of H syllables 'go against the pitch accent tendencies of the rest of the language'.
